definition: Lenient means mild and merciful rather than strict.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word lenient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know lenient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Traffic court is lenient with first offenses here, trading the fine for a Saturday morning safety class.

Easygoing is milder than lenient — an easygoing coach is simply relaxed by nature, before any rule is broken, while lenient describes an authority who faces a real offense and chooses the merciful penalty.
Permissive goes further than lenient — the lenient judge softens the punishment, while the permissive one has all but stopped enforcing the rule.

A forgiving person is quick to excuse a wrong once it is done, letting go of the grudge — anyone can be forgiving, power or none. Lenient belongs to someone who holds the power to punish: a lenient judge still hands down a penalty, just the mild and merciful one.

Soft is the schoolyard word for the same mildness, and it smuggles in a hint of weakness — the soft referee gets walked over. Lenient carries no such insult: a lenient authority has the power to be strict and deliberately chooses mercy where mercy is deserved.

Latin lenis, 'soft,' left almost no other footprint in everyday English — its few descendants, like the medical lenitive, stayed on pharmacy shelves. So lenient stands alone: learn the leni- and you have learned the whole family.
Lenient means mild and merciful rather than strict.
Curfew at the Otero house is ten, and Sam came in at midnight.
His mother heard the whole story — the dead phone, the missed bus, the long walk — and was lenient, handing down nothing worse than an earlier curfew for the next week.
His friends, grounded for a month over less, could not believe his luck.
Lenient is the exact word for the mother, because lenient means mild and merciful rather than strict — the authority is hers, the punishment was earned, and she chose the soft end of the scale.
Soft alone can mean weak; a lenient judge is not weak, just sparing where sparing seems right.
Lenient belongs to people with the power to punish: judges, teachers, referees, parents.
Its unit-mates sit close but differ — forbearance keeps your own cool when provoked, accommodating bends plans to fit others, and tactful softens words rather than punishments.
Negligent is the false friend: a lenient judge chooses mildness; a negligent one simply stopped paying attention.

Ojeda took over the library, the fine drawer held decades of grudges.
Her predecessor had chased every overdue nickel and revoked cards over a single late book.
Ojeda announced a different policy her first week.
Late books would still cost something — she was clear that the rules mattered — but the penalty became a canned good for the food pantry per week overdue.
Patrons tested her at first, and she did not let everything slide: chronic offenders still lost borrowing privileges for a month.
The staff came to describe her as lenient rather than lax.
She held all the power the old rules gave her; she simply chose penalties that stung a little and taught more.
